subject: Computer Networking
title: Tonga's Cable Cut (2022)
description: A quick win: understand Tonga's Cable Cut (2022).

hook.text: On January 15, 2022, a volcanic eruption severed Tonga's only internet cable. The nation went dark.

buildup.text: Tonga depends on a single undersea fiber cable. When the eruption damaged it, no backup path existed.

discovery.text: Satellites provided minimal bandwidth — enough for emergency messages, not normal internet use.

twist.text: Repair took five weeks. A specialized ship sailed from Papua New Guinea to reach the break point.

climax.text: The outage exposed island nations' fragility. Redundancy is a luxury not all countries can afford.

punchline.text: One cable, one volcano, five weeks of silence.

quiz.question: How long did it take to restore Tonga's internet after the cable was cut?

details.summary: In January 2022, the eruption of the Hunga Tonga volcano severed Tonga's only undersea fiber optic cable, cutting the island nation off from the internet for over five weeks. The disaster exposed how countries with limited cable redundancy can be completely isolated by a single physical event.
details.whyItMatters: Tonga's disconnection showed that for island nations with only one cable, losing that cable means losing all connectivity. Physical redundancy is a matter of national resilience.
takeaways: A volcanic eruption severed Tonga's only internet cable
The nation was offline for over five weeks awaiting repair
Limited satellite backup provided minimal emergency connectivity

faq.question: Why didn't satellite internet cover for the cable?
faq.answer: Satellite connections were available but provided only a fraction of the bandwidth the cable carried. They could support emergency government communications but not normal internet usage for the population. Satellite cannot fully replace undersea cable capacity.

faq.question: How was Tonga's cable repaired?
faq.answer: A specialized cable repair ship had to travel to the region, locate the damage across the volcanic debris field, and splice the fiber. The entire process took over five weeks due to the ship's transit time and the complexity of working near active volcanic deposits.
